paper_title: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time Jianyu Wu1,2 Yizhou Wang2,3 Encheng Su2,4 Jinouwen Zhang2 Pengze Li2,5 Lintao Wang2,6 Chen Tang2,3 Aoran Wang2 Wanli Ouyang3 Shixiang Tang2,3,* 1Shanghai Jiao Tong University 2Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory 3The Chinese University of Hong Kong 4The University of Science and Technology of China 5Fudan University 6The University of Sydney *Corresponding author wujianyu@sjtu.edu.cn tangshixiang@pjlab.org.cn Figure 1: Self-Consistency vs. TT-RSI. At test time, model must judge its own answers on unlabeled questions, with no ground truth to tell which to trust. (a) Self-consistency-based methods resolve this by majority voting, taking the most frequent answer as the final output and as the training target, leaving prior reasoning unused at inference and reinforcing wrong answers during training. (b) TT-RSI reuses reasoning for efficient inference and trains on self-improvement to strengthen answering and refinement.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Enabling AI systems to improve their own capabilities (e.g., recursive self-improvement (Novikov et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) and continual learning (Ye et al., 2026)) is central to progress toward artificial general intelligence (Schmidhuber, 2007; Silver and Sutton, 2025). For LLMs, test time is natural setting for such improvement: after 1 model is deployed, the goal is to answer new, unlabeled questions more accurately using only selfgenerated signals. Two families of methods pursue this goal: test-time scaling spends more inference compute on each question (Snell et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025), while test-time training updates the models weights on unlabeled test questions (Sun et al., 2020; Zuo et al., 2025). Ideally, the two form loop: better answers train better model, which in turn produces better answers, allowing improvements to accumulate over successive rounds without external supervision. However, current test-time methods rely primarily on Self-Consistency (SC) for both inference and training: they sample independent solutions and use majority voting either to select the final answer (Wang et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2024) or to construct training targets (Zuo et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Gkountouras et al., 2026). This leads to two linked limitations: (1) Inefficient inference. Each attempt starts from scratch and leaves earlier reasoning unused, so additional compute yields more independent samples rather than better reasoning. (2) Unreliable supervision. Majority voting rewards whichever answer the model already produces most often, so when that majority is wrong, training reinforces the error. Together, these limitations break the loop above, so test-time improvement stalls rather than accumulates. In contrast, humans tackle difficult problems by building on earlier attempts, retaining useful reasoning, revising mistakes, and gradually improving their problem-solving strategies (Pólya, 1945). Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), label-free framework that improves LLMs at test time through both inference and training (Figure 1). Both rely on an improvement step, which re-solves question with the previous solution as context. Specifically, at inference, additional compute builds on earlier reasoning instead of repeating it. During training, the model learns from its own refinements rather than majority votes. Since refinement can fix an earlier attempt even when most attempts agree on wrong answer, this supervision can move the model beyond its initial majority, yielding higher accuracy than majority-based training while preserving the gains from further test-time scaling. TT-RSI realizes the improvement step through two complementary components. At inference, we introduce In-Context RSI, training-free test-time scaling strategy that turns additional compute into successive refinements. Given question, the LLM first generates an initial solution, then repeatedly re-solves the question with its latest solution as context, and returns the final answer of the last attempt. However, simply conditioning on previous solutions can restrict exploration and cause repetition (Gu et al., 2026; Rance et al., 2026). We therefore present the full solution neutrally, preserving its intermediate reasoning while letting the LLM decide whether and how to use it. With the previous solution in view, the LLM need not rederive every step: it can keep verified steps, focus on questionable ones, and avoid repeating earlier dead ends. As result, In-Context RSI surpasses self-consistency while reducing generated tokens by relative 68.6% (Figure 3). These successive solutions also serve as training signals. During training, we introduce In-Weight RSI, label-free test-time training method that distills the gains of In-Context RSI into the models weights. In-Weight RSI uses the first attempt and its immediate refinement, pair of adjacent solutions from an In-Context RSI chain generated by the current policy, as references, strengthening both answering and refinement while transferring later improvements into the first attempt. Concretely, it learns from these references through on-policy selfdistillation (OPSD; Zhao et al., 2026a), which turns them into token-level guidance on the models own rollouts. Because each refinement re-examines the full previous derivation, it can correct intermediate steps even when the final answer remains wrong. Token-level guidance captures such partial corrections, which majority voting over final answers cannot. In this way, In-Context RSI and In-Weight RSI reinforce each other: the refinements of In-Context RSI train better model through In-Weight RSI, and the updated model refines more effectively under In-Context RSI, generating stronger references for later training. This realizes the ideal loop between test-time scaling and training described above, so improvements can be accumulated without external supervision. We validate TT-RSI with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B and 8B (Yang et al., 2025a) on five competition mathematics benchmarks (Balunovic et al., 2025; Dekoninck et al., 2026) against five label-free baselines. In-Weight RSI and the full TT-RSI improve average accuracy over the base model by +5.79% and +13.89%, respectively. Under the same testtime scaling budget, TT-RSI exceeds the strongest self-consistency-based method, TTPO + SC (Wang 2 Figure 2: Overview of TT-RSI. In-Context RSI generates a1 from q, then repeatedly re-solves given the full previous solution. The model autonomously chooses what to reuse, rework, or solve anew, producing a2, . . . , aℓ. In-Weight RSI uses these solutions as teacher references: Recursive Distillation combines a1and a2-conditioned guidance for answering (Lans) and refinement (Lref ) as LRec. Accelerated Distillation compares the a1and a2-conditioned guidance on y0 and weights only a2 guidance (LAcc), with larger shifts receiving larger weights. The updated policy starts the next refinement chain. et al., 2026), by +4.79% on average. Our contributions are as follows: recursive self-improvement framework. We propose TT-RSI, which goes beyond selfconsistency by using self-improvement for both test-time scaling and label-free test-time training. Two mutually reinforcing components. We design In-Context RSI to let the model build on its full previous solution, and In-Weight RSI to distill successive refinements into answering and refinement, so that each strengthens the other. Theory and experiments. We prove that distilling from two successive solutions strengthens refinement and moves the first attempt toward the infinite-step limit, and demonstrate accuracy and token-efficiency gains empirically.

sections.title: 3 Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement
sections.content: TT-RSI applies the improvement step (Section 3.1) in two components: In-Context RSI (Section 3.2) repeats it to refine answers at inference, while InWeight RSI (Section 3.3) turns the resulting refine3 ments into supervision for answering and refinement (Figure 2). 3.1 The improvement step At the core of TT-RSI is an improvement step, which lets the model improve on its own attempts without labels by turning completed attempt into context for further reasoning. previous solution provides starting point from which the model can reuse useful parts of an argument, reconsider intermediate steps, and develop better solution. Starting from a1 πθ( q), repeated application gives ak+1 πθ( q, ak). Only the latest solution ak is carried forward, so the sequence forms Markov chain without an expanding history. Because later solutions tend to improve on earlier ones (Figure 3), they can also supervise earlier attempts during training, distilling later improvements into the model (Section 3.3). Further details of the refinement setup are provided in Appendix B. 3.2 In-Context RSI Even an unsuccessful attempt often contains correct intermediate steps, yet independent sampling discards them and starts each attempt from scratch. To put them to use, we propose In-Context RSI, training-free test-time scaling strategy that applies the improvement step repeatedly to the same question, so that each attempt builds on the previous one. Effective refinement needs information from an earlier attempt and the freedom to reconsider it. Yet conditioning too strongly on an earlier solution can suppress exploration and lead to repeated solutions (Gu et al., 2026; Rance et al., 2026). Directly applying correction-oriented feedback can also induce unnecessary changes to correct answer (Huang et al., 2024; Kamoi et al., 2024). To address this tension, In-Context RSI combines full-solution references with autonomous reference use. Given q, the policy first generates an initial solution a1 πθ( q). Each subsequent attempt then receives full-solution reference: the complete previous solution ak, including both its step-by-step derivation and its final answer, rather than the final answer alone. Attempt ak+1 can thus check the individual steps of ak, keep those that hold, and locate where the derivation went wrong, so even solution with an incorrect final answer contributes reusable steps. For autonomous reference use, we present ak neutrally as previous attempt, without indicating whether it is correct or requesting corrections, and ask the policy to solve the problem independently (Appendix B). The policy itself decides how to use each part of ak: reuse it, rework it, or take new approach. Repeating this step yields chain a1 a2 aℓ of one initial solution and ℓ1 refinements, and we return the final answer of aℓ. To characterize the balance between correcting and preserving answers, we use two-state model (Yang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025; He et al., 2025). Each refinement step corrects wrong answer with probability , the fix rate, and breaks correct one with probability b, the break rate. Proposition 1. For constant fix/break rates with +b (0, 1], In-Context RSI improves its firstattempt accuracy acc1 exactly when (1acc1) > acc1. Its limiting accuracy, the balance point, is /(f +b). refinement design should therefore raise the fix rate relative to the break rate. We compare these rates for In-Context RSI and its design variants in Section 4.3. 3. In-Weight RSI The improvements of In-Context RSI last only for the current question, and majority-vote targets can reinforce wrong answer. We therefore propose InWeight RSI, label-free test-time training method that distills successive refinements into the models weights. Taking the first two solutions a1, a2 of an In-Context RSI chain generated by πθ as references, In-Weight RSI trains answering and refinement through Recursive Distillation and couples them through Accelerated Distillation, optimizing both objectives jointly. Both use OPSD (Eq. (1)), with these references as privileged information. Recursive Distillation. key design question is which solution along the refinement chain should supervise which attempt. Ideally, training would transfer the result of infinitely many refinements directly into the first attempt, absorbing the full benefit of the chain. However, long chains are costly to generate, and their late solutions can differ substantially from the students early attempts, making the teachers guidance on the students own rollouts less reliable. This raises question: is it possible to supervise only local relationships along the chain and thereby avoid these issues? Fortunately, the chain involves only two behaviors: answering the question and refining the previous attempt. Every later step reuses the refinement operation, so training these two behaviors covers 4 the recurring roles along the chain. For each behavior, we sample student rollout: y0 πθ( q) for answering and y1 πθ( q, a1) for refinement. The teacher receives a1 for answering and a2 in place of a1 for refinement: Lans = D(cid:0) sg[πθ0( q, a1)] πθ( q)(cid:1), Lref = D(cid:0) sg[πθ0( q, a2)] πθ( q, a1)(cid:1). (2) The losses are evaluated on y0 and y1, respectively. We call Lans answer distillation: its teacher has already seen a1, so it transfers one improvement step into the first attempt. We call Lref refinement distillation: its teacher has seen the refined solution a2, so it trains the improvement step to incorporate further refinement. We combine them as LRec = Lans + Lref . (3) Although LRec needs only two reference solutions per question, it can recover the effect of much longer chains over repeated updates. After each update, both behaviors improve, so the references a1, a2 generated by the updated policy correspond to later attempts of the original chain. Distilling them again moves the first attempt and each refinement step further along that chain. Each update thus needs only one-step-ahead targets, while the gains compound across updates (Theorem 1). Accelerated Distillation. Lans and Lref remain loosely coupled: the first attempt does not receive direct supervision from the later reference a2. Accelerated Distillation connects them by supervising the first-attempt rollout y0 with the a2-conditioned teacher of refinement distillation: LAcc = Dω (cid:0) sg[πθ0( q, a2)] πθ( q)(cid:1). (4) Because Lans already supplies a1-conditioned guidance, we emphasize what changes when the reference is refined to a2. We compare the teachers next-token distributions under a1 and a2 at the same prefix y0,<t, and define the guidance shift dt from a1 to a2 as the total-variation distance between them. It determines the token weight ωt = 1 α + 2α dt dt + τ , (5) where 0 < α < 1 controls the weighting strength and τ > 0 sets the change scale. Dω multiplies each tokens distillation loss on y0 by ωt. Larger shifts strengthen the a2-conditioned supervision at positions affected by refinement. In total, In-Weight RSI minimizes = LRec + wAccLAcc, (6) where wAcc weights Accelerated Distillation. Theoretical analysis. To understand how the two local distillation terms recover longer refinement chains, we model sequence-level distillation with exact distributional backups, following the one-step bootstrap structure of temporal-difference learning (Bellman, 1957; Sutton, 1988). Theorem 1 (Compression and amplification). After exact distributional backups of Recursive Distillation, the models k-th attempt matches the initial models (n+1)k-th attempt in distribution. Answer distillation compresses later attempts into the first, while refinement distillation makes each refinement step equivalent to n+1 initial-model steps. Accelerated Distillation lets the first attempt use this strengthened refinement operation directly, accumulating its gains across updates. Proposition 2 (Accelerated Distillation). Accelerated Distillation makes the first attempt mixture of initial-model attempts whose expected index grows quadratically with the number of exact backups. Together, these results show that local supervision strengthens refinement and moves the first attempt toward the initial models infinite-step refinement limit, with Accelerated Distillation speeding the transfer (proofs in Appendix A). In-Context RSI and In-Weight RSI thus close the loop: teacher guidance strengthens answering and refinement, and the updated policy generates the next reference solutions. This turns test-time compute into lasting model improvement without external labels.

sections.content: We compare TT-RSI with existing label-free testtime training methods (Section 4.2), then ablate its components (Section 4.3) and analyze its gains and costs (Section 4.4).

sections.title: 4.2 Main results
sections.content: First, under the same test-time scaling budget, TTRSI outperforms self-consistency-based test-time training at every model scale (see Table 1). On average, it exceeds TTPO + SC by +4.79%, with wins in 11 of the 15 settings and ties in two. On AIME26 at 8B, for example, accuracy is 86.67%, compared with 73.33% for TTPO + SC (+13.34%). The best accuracy and balance point are in bold. reproduce the same error: in the same setting, selfconsistency lifts TTPO by only +2.50%, whereas In-Context RSI lifts Base by +8.89%. Training on refinements instead strengthens revision, improving the solutions that later attempts build on. Second, even without test-time scaling, InWeight RSI achieves the best first-attempt accuracy among label-free training methods at every model scale. It improves over Base by +5.79% on average, beating all five training baselines in 13 of the 15 settings and tying for the best score in one other. At 8B, its mean accuracy is 64.17%, +2.34% above TTPO (Wang et al., 2026), the strongest training baseline on average. These gains show that distillation retains refinement benefits in the model and remains effective with stronger starting policy. Third, the gains from training also carry over to inference-time refinement. Specifically, the full framework gains +13.89% over Base and exceeds Base + In-Context RSI by +7.33%. In-Weight RSI therefore helps even when in-context improvement is available at inference, raising both the first and later attempts. Notably, at 1.7B, the first attempt of In-Weight RSI (41.99%) already exceeds Base + In-Context RSI after ten refinements (39.73%), consistent with the compression of later attempts into the first attempt (Theorem 1).

The full design raises mean accuracy from 53.84% to 63.59% after ten refinement steps. Directing reference use lowers accuracy (3.16%) and the fix rate, suggesting that autonomous use leaves more room to correct earlier mistakes. The balance points reflect the same pattern. Unrelated references have the highest fix rate but also introduce frequent regressions, yielding the lowest balance point. Full-solution references and autonomous use balance correction with preservation, giving In-Context RSI the highest balance point. Mutual reinforcement across updates. We compare references generated by the current and initial policies under the same distillation objective (see Table 3b). Generating references with the evolving policy improves first-attempt accuracy by +1.67% on AIME26 and +3.79% on HMMT26 over using the fixed initial policy. After ten refinement steps, the advantages are +8.89% and +3.79%, respectively. Evolving references therefore improve both the first and final attempts. This matches the bootstrap analysis (Theorem 1): fixed initial-policy references always provide the same one-step targets, whereas evolving references let the gains compound across updates. Together with the stronger refinement observed after training (Section 4.2), this shows how improvements in the policy and its references reinforce one another. without further updates  (Table 4)  . Compared with Base, mean target accuracy improves by +2.37% and +3.05%, respectively. In-Weight RSI achieves the highest accuracy on all six sourcetarget pairs, averaging 59.64% and exceeding OPSD-TTT, the strongest baseline on average. These transfer gains show that the improvement is retained in the model weights and applies to new questions. Gains beyond the initial majority. To test whether refinement-based training can overcome an initially wrong majority, we evaluate the In-Weight RSI model and the baselines with 64 independent answers per question on AIME26, focusing on the six questions whose Base majority is wrong (Table 5a), where avg@64 averages the 64 answers and SC@64 is their majority vote. Several selfconsistency-based baselines perform below Base on this subset, illustrating how training on agreement can reinforce an initially wrong answer. On these questions, In-Weight RSI raises avg@64 from 5.73% to 12.76% (+7.03%), exceeding OPSDTTTs 8.33% by +4.43%. Self-consistency also becomes correct on two of these questions, compared with one for OPSD-TTT. Overall avg@64 improves by +4.79% over Base and +3.69% over OPSD-TTT, the strongest baseline in this comparison. This demonstrates that training on refinements raises accuracy on questions whose majority is wrong, not only on those the model already answers correctly by majority. Cross-task transfer. At comparable total token cost, it retains an accuracy advantage of +2.13%. Training efficiency. To measure the training cost of the improvement loop, we compare methods with 32 question occurrences per update on four H20 GPUs (Table 5b). With pipelined reference generation, In-Weight RSI takes 8.53 minutes on AIME26 and 10.06 on HMMT26, giving speedup of 2.295.36 per update over the baselines. Selfconsistency fails because its most frequent answer, produced by three of eleven samples, comes from flawed averaging argument and outvotes the two samples reaching the correct 63/256, while base refinement succeeds by replacing that argument with recurrence for S(n), the expected sum of squared piece lengths. sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our evaluation covers mathematical reasoning and the Qwen3 family up to 8B parameters. broader direction is to extend TT-RSI to open-ended tasks and tool-using agents, where improvement unfolds over interactions and must be retained across tasks.

sections.title: 5 Related work
sections.content: Test-time scaling. Parallel scaling aggregates independent solutions (Wang et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2024), while sequential methods build on earlier attempts by revision or re-solving (Madaan et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2025). Repetition and limited exploration can restrict these gains (Gu et al., 2026; Rance et al., 2026). Compute can also be allocated within single attempt, by its reasoning length (Guo et al., 2025) or by the effective depth of the architecture (Liang et al., 2026), rather than by the number of attempts. In-Context RSI preserves exploration by letting the model decide whether and how to use full-solution references, and InWeight RSI distills the resulting refinements. Label-free test-time training. This line of work adapts models on unlabeled test inputs using selfgenerated supervision (Sun et al., 2020; Akyürek et al., 2025). TTRL rewards majority agreement (Zuo et al., 2025), and TTPO distills solutions selected by self-consistency (Wang et al., 2026). Other methods use agreement to select teacher references (Gkountouras et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026) or sharpen confidence (Zhao et al., 2026b; Agarwal et al., 2025). In-Weight RSI uses successive solutions as teacher references, obtaining guidance from refinement rather than majority agreement. Self-improvement and distillation. Training on self-generated attempts has been studied with correctness feedback (Zelikman et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2025) and in recursive training frameworks (Lee et al., 2026), which recent survey organizes by how far the improvement loop is closed (Chen et al., 2026). Recent systems evolve algorithms and agents (Novikov et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) or consolidate deployment experience into model parameters (Ye et al., 2026). On-policy self-distillation uses contextual information to construct dense teacher supervision (Zhao et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026). TT-RSI connects in-context improvement with weight updates by distilling successive self-generated refinements, forming test-time amplify-then-distill loop (Anthony et al., 2017; Christiano et al., 2018).

Additional pairs repeat the same refinement target while requiring longer reference chains. We retain the first two adjacent pairs and compare third in Table 3. Self-Consistency and self-improvement. Methods based on majority-conditioned supervision (Zuo et al., 2025; Gkountouras et al., 2026) or probability sharpening (Agarwal et al., 2025; Prabhudesai et al., 2026) favor answers that already dominate the models predictions, which can reinforce an incorrect majority. Training on successive reference solutions instead gives the refinement backup, which approaches π. Its accuracy depends on the correction and preservation behavior of rather than the initial mode. The comparison on questions with an incorrect initial majority in Table 5a examines this distinction empirically.

sections.title: B Prompts
sections.content: Question-only prompt. Evaluation and the first attempt use the plain question prompt: {question} Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. Improvement template. The improvement step of Section 3.1 uses: {question} previous attempt at solving this problem was: {previous solution} Please solve the problem independently. Reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. The reference ak is the previous visible solution, including its reasoning process and final answer. For reasoning models, ak excludes the hidden thinking trace, which is not carried forward.

sections.title: D Baseline details
sections.content: TTPO. Following the released implementation (Wang et al., 2026), TTPO selects eight training trajectories from 64 non-thinking candidates per question. teacher conditioned on the majority answer supervises agreeing trajectories through SoftOR-weighted forward KL, while group-relative policy-gradient term penalizes disagreements. TTRL. TTRL optimizes the policy with GRPO using agreement with the sampled majority as its reward (Zuo et al., 2025). In the training-cost comparison, it generates eight thinking trajectories per question and reuses each batch for two updates. OPSD-TTT. OPSD-TTT uses the current policys generated final answer to condition frozen initial-model teacher (Wang et al., 2026). The teacher supervises one non-thinking student rollout per question through clipped forward KL. LoRA and optimizer settings follow Table 6. CANON. CANON samples 32 solutions per question and selects the solution with the highest mean token log-probability among those reaching the majority answer (Gkountouras et al., 2026). This full solution conditions frozen teacher, and the question-only student is trained with Jensen Shannon divergence over the sampled rollouts. U-OPSD. U-OPSD samples eight rollouts per question and uses majority-agreeing solution as the teachers reference to supervise disagreeing rollouts through clipped forward KL (Li et al., 2026). The training-cost comparison uses thinking mode for generation and distillation. Comparison setup. All baselines use the same starting checkpoints and unlabeled benchmark questions as In-Weight RSI, with final boxed answers graded by math-verify. The training-cost comparison in Table 5b uses Qwen3-4B on four H20 GPUs, with 100 updates and 32 question occurrences per update. As in all other experiments, In-Weight RSI uses pipelined references and τ = 104. Test-time scaling budget. Under the same testtime scaling budget, TTPO + SC generates as many tokens per question as TT-RSI uses to reach its final attempt, i.e., the initial solution and ten refinements. In-Context RSI also reads the previous solution at each step. Because ak excludes the hidden thinking trace (Appendix B), it averages fewer than 1,000 tokens, far fewer than those generated per attempt (Figure 3). We therefore count only generated tokens and treat this input cost as negligible.
